title: JPMorgan Rethinks UK Investments: Will Higher Taxes Hurt Growth? - TradingView
content: JPMorgan JPM is reportedly reconsidering its planned investments in the United Kingdom as higher banking taxes threaten to weigh on profitability. The bank is evaluating potential spending reductions at its Bournemouth operations center and approximately £5 billion Canary Wharf development in London. However, neither project is likely to be abandoned. The development follows CEO Jamie Dimon's Nov. 20 remarks about offsetting the financial impact of higher taxes. The U.K. banking surcharge is set to double from 3% to 6% for 15 months, beginning January 2027. The measure could increase JPMorgan's tax bill by £120 million, affecting after-tax earnings and investment returns. Potential spending reductions underscore the company's focus on disciplined capital allocation and expense management. Scaling back infrastructure investments could help preserve cash flows and moderate future operating costs. JPMorgan may also reassess the geographical allocation of incremental investments, prioritizing markets offering more attractive risk-adjusted returns. However, significantly curtailing U.K. investments could pose challenges. London remains a major global financial hub, offering access to institutional clients, skilled professionals and international capital markets. Reduced spending could limit JPMorgan's ability to expand operational capacity and capitalize on emerging business opportunities in the region. JPMorgan's diversified revenue streams and robust earnings generation provide flexibility to absorb incremental tax costs. While disciplined spending could cushion the financial impact, prolonged tax uncertainty and reduced infrastructure investments may constrain international expansion. Management's ability to balance expense optimization with strategic investments will remain crucial to sustaining long-term earnings growth and shareholder returns. JPMorgan’s Peers & Their Global Expansion Initiatives Two key peers of JPM are Bank of America BAC and Goldman Sachs GS. Bank of America is strengthening its international presence through strategic hiring and broader corporate banking coverage. Bank of America has doubled its corporate banking team across Europe, the Middle East and Africa, targeting 40% client growth in the region to capitalize on cross-border financing and advisory opportunities. Goldman continues to strengthen its international operations through workforce expansion across key financial and technology hubs. Goldman added 142 employees to its European banking operations over the past year, while its Indian workforce exceeds 8,000, supporting global operational capabilities and business expansion. title: JPM Says High-risk Debt Ratio of HK Property Developers Falls to 30%; Top Picks LINK REIT, SWIREPROPERTIES; HSBC HOLDINGS, STANCHART Preferred for Banks - TradingView
content: JPMorgan updated its risk assessment on 53 Hong Kong-listed property companies using data for 1H26. The proportion of high-risk debt improved faintly to 30% from 34% in FY2024, on lower financing costs. Apart from NEW WORLD DEV 17, credit indicators of major property developers remained broadly solid. The proportion of high-risk debt among mid-sized and small property developers improved to 61% and 66%, respectively, from the previous 72%-77%. The overall net gearing ratio improved to 18% in 1H26 from 20% in FY2025, the broker noted. Short-term debt cash coverage slightly deteriorated to 1.5x from 1.6x, while OCF coverage on interest expense edged down to 3.5x from 3.6x. If HIBOR rises by 200 bps, interest expenses of property developers were estimated to hike by about 23% on average, and the proportion of debt with operating cash flow interest coverage below 2x would rise from 29% to 47%. Assuming operating cash flow declines by 30%, the ratio would increase from 29% to 61%. Among major property developers, JPMorgan reclassified HENDERSON LAND 12 and KERRY PPT 683 from medium risk to low risk, although they would return to medium risk if interest rates rise by 200 bps. JPMorgan preferred landlords and expects home prices to decline by less than 5% by 2027, while office rents and retail sales are expected to rise by up to 5%. Its top picks were LINK REIT 823, SWIREPROPERTIES 1972 and Hongkong Land, followed by CK ASSET 1113, which is in a net cash position. The bank maintained a cautious stance on NEW WORLD DEV 17, citing liquidity pressure has yet to ease significantly and that the company remains the most sensitive to interest rates. On banks, JPMorgan viewed risks related to Hong Kong commercial real estate remain manageable. The proportion of Hong Kong commercial real estate loans to total loans declined from 16% in 2024 to 12% by the end of 3Q26. The weighted average Stage 3 loan ratio fell HoH by 55 bps to 10.2% in 1H26. About 64% of Hong Kong commercial real estate loans are secured. Even if collateral values decline by 30%, the estimated risky debt ratio would be 5.5%-7.6%, lower than the weighted average Stage 3 loan ratio of 10%. JPMorgan preferred STANCHART 2888 and HSBC HOLDINGS 5. In comparison, BOC HONG KONG 2388's Stage 3 loan ratio for HK CRE loans was only 1.9%. Select market data provided by ICE Data Services. title: JPM Upgrades LI AUTO-W to Neutral, Raises TP to HKD40 as 3Q Results Beat - TradingView
content: JPMorgan published a research report on LI AUTO-W 2015, of which 3Q results beat, with gross margin and net profit both starkly beating the broker's and market forecasts, on the back of improved product mix and cost efficiency. JPMorgan closed its Underweight rating and upgraded the stock to Neutral. The H-share TP was raised from HKD35 to HKD40, while the ADR TP for Li Auto Inc. LI was lifted from USD9 to USD10. The broker noted that the i6 and L6 models will help support sales volume growth, while the premium L8 and i9 models will drive margin expansion. Overseas sales were estimated to double YoY from a low base, with management forecasting overseas sales to more than double YoY next year. Following the L9's entry into the UAE market, shipments of the i6 to the EU were expected to commence in 1Q27. JPMorgan predicted accelerated overseas expansion to provide upside momentum for Li Auto's sales and earnings next year, while the company is also promoting localized sales and after-sales services. In addition, a longer vehicle facelift cycle (extended to two years) was expected to reduce R&D expenses and help operating cash flow and FCF turn positive for full-year 2027. title: JP Morgan Outlines Oil Outlook for 2027, 2028 - Rigzone
content:
In a new report sent to Rigzone by Natasha Kaneva, J.P. Morgan’s Head of Global Commodities Strategy, analysts at the company, including Kaneva, outlined J.P. Morgan’s oil outlook for 2027 and 2028. The J.P. Morgan analysts revealed in the report that their outlook assumes the U.S.-Iran and Russia-Ukraine conflicts continue, “yet oil keeps moving and the global market remains in surplus”. “If 2022 and 2026 have taught us anything, it is that wars can disrupt oil flows without stopping them,” the analysts said in the report. “We are therefore modeling a world in which two wars continue, but oil keeps moving,” they added. The analysts highlighted in the report that, “with crude flowing and demand contracting, the global oil market returned to surplus in September”. They pointed out that this excess widened in October and that China has already begun rebuilding its crude inventories, “adding 400,000 barrels per day in October” with the country “on pace to add another 500,000 barrels per day in November”. “We expect that surplus to persist into 2027,” the analysts revealed. “Our forecast assumes Middle Eastern oil flows remain near 90 percent of pre-war levels through March, rising to 94 percent by June and 98 percent by year-end, while demand returns sustainably to pre-war volumes by August,” they added. “China is expected to rebuild crude inventories at an average pace of nearly 700,000 barrels per day, with OECD countries adding another 400,000 barrels per day,” they projected. They warned, however, that, even after accounting for this stock-building, they project a global surplus of 1.6 million barrels per day, “consistent with a Brent price in the high $70s in the first half of the year and the high $60s in the second”. The analysts went on to warn that this surplus will not disappear in 2028. “Even assuming China accelerates inventory accumulation to 1.1 million barrels per day and OECD countries continue adding 0.4 million barrels per day, we expect the market to remain oversupplied by roughly 1.4 million barrels per day, implying a Brent price in the mid-$60s,” they said. “That is our fundamentally driven price forecast, not necessarily the price at which oil will trade throughout the year,” the analysts highlighted, noting that further escalations “could inject substantial geopolitical risk premia into the market”. The J.P. Morgan analysts revealed in the report that they are reluctant to forecast those premia, “let alone embed them permanently into our price outlook”. “History suggests they can be large, but rarely last,” they pointed out. “Since 2005, monthly Brent prices have never exceeded our estimated fair value by more than $24 per barrel, with such deviations lasting an average of just 3.8 months,” they said. “Two wars may keep oil prices volatile. But unless they materially alter the physical balance, the underlying surplus should ultimately prevail,” they projected. The J.P. Morgan analysts highlighted in the report that a “flood of supply is coming”, pointing out that global liquids production “is projected to surge by nearly eight million barrels per day in 2027, reaching 109 million barrels per day, before climbing to 110 million barrels per day by year-end and remaining near that level in 2028”. In their report, the analysts outlined that the U.S.-Iran conflict “has acted like a dam, holding back Middle Eastern production for months”. “Once the barriers are lifted, the rush to reclaim lost market share could unleash a flood of additional supply, particularly from producers outside Iran,” they projected. “By March 2027, we expect Middle Eastern supply outside of Iran to have fully recovered to its 2025 average, before rising further,” they said. The Middle East will not be alone in driving supply growth, according to the analysts, who projected that the Americas are set to add another 1.6 million barrels per day to supply, led by a 0.5 million barrel per day increase in U.S. total liquids production. “Brazil should contribute another 0.5 million barrels per day, as three new floating production, storage and offloading vessels come online, with output expected to keep rising through 2031,” they said. “Guyana should add 0.3 million barrels per day, while Canada and Argentina will contribute another 0.1 and 0.2 million barrels per day, respectively,” they added. “Importantly, much of the growth in Brazil and Guyana comes from deep-water projects, where production is relatively insensitive to oil prices and unlikely to slow even if prices weaken,” they continued. The analysts went on to warn that Russia “remains the main geopolitical variable”. “Assuming the war in Ukraine continues without a resolution, we expect Russian production to average 8.7 million barrels per day next year, broadly unchanged from current levels,” they said. “A ceasefire, however, could lift output to 9.4 million barrels per day, adding another 0.7 million barrels per day to global supply,” they added. “Put these numbers together, and the scale of the recovery becomes extraordinary. After plunging from 107 million barrels per day in 2025 to 101 million barrels per day in 2026, global liquids production is poised to surge to 109 million barrels per day in 2027,” they noted. “That is nearly eight million barrels per day of additional supply in a single year, more than reversing the losses of 2026 and leaving the world producing two million barrels per day more oil than before the war,” they added. “In just twelve months, the world could emerge from one of the largest supply disruptions in history with more oil than it had going into it,” they continued. “And the recovery is unlikely to stop there”, the analysts emphasized. “We project global oil supply to reach 110 million barrels per day by the end of 2027 and remain near that level throughout 2028 - some three million barrels per day above its 2025 average and an extraordinary nine million barrels per day above 2019 levels,” they added. The J.P. Morgan analysts projected in the report that oil demand will rebound but said refining capacity will set the ceiling for this comeback. “Oil consumption could theoretically recover by 4.5 million barrels per day in 2027 but meeting that demand would require global refinery runs to increase by 4.1 million barrels per day relative to 2026, against an expected gain of just 3.3 million barrels per day,” they said. “Refining constraints will keep product cracks and prices elevated, limiting demand growth to 3.5 million barrels per day, just 0.6 million barrels per day above pre-war levels,” they added. The analysts went on to reveal in the report that, “with demand data now available through September”, they estimate that global oil consumption has fallen by 3.0 million barrels per day this year. “Nearly half of that decline - 1.3 million barrels per day - came from petrochemical feedstocks, as physical shortages forced refiners to cut runs, particularly in Asia,” they said. “The rest was largely a response to record-high regional prices for refined products, rather than crude oil itself, with diesel demand falling by 0.8 million barrels per day, gasoline by 0.5 million barrels per day and jet fuel by 0.1 million barrels per day,” they added. “The Middle East, at the center of the conflict, saw consumption fall by 0.9 million barrels per day, while China and the rest of Asia each lost roughly 0.8 million barrels per day as shortages and soaring product prices took their toll,” they continued. “The impact eventually spread to developed economies, including Europe, where consumption contracted by 0.28 million barrels per day and the U.S., where it declined by 0.13 million barrels per day,” they noted. The analysts stated in the report that “why consumption fell matters enormously for what comes next”. “If demand has fallen primarily because oil products were unavailable or prohibitively expensive, much of that consumption should return once supplies normalize and prices retreat,” they said. “And although the conflict is now in its ninth month, we doubt it has lasted long enough to fundamentally reshape consumption patterns,” they added. “Still, there is a limit to how much stretching even a rubber band can withstand. The longer consumers are forced to adapt to shortages and high prices, the greater the risk that some of those adjustments will become permanent,” they continued. The J.P. Morgan analysts said in the report that, “for now”, their “natural inclination is to follow the conventional logic of hysteresis”. “After major economic shocks and disruptions, oil consumption tends to recover toward its previous level, but the subsequent growth trajectory becomes shallower. In other words, the level of demand recovers, but some of its future growth is lost,” they added. The mechanism for that recovery is relatively straightforward, according to the analysts. “As damaged refining capacity returns and refinery runs normalize, product shortages should ease, refining cracks should retreat and trade flows recover,” they said. “Lower product prices, in turn, should encourage consumption that was previously constrained by either availability or affordability,” they added. “Following this logic, global oil demand could in theory rebound like a coiled spring, surging by as much as 4.5 million barrels per day in 2027, lifting consumption 1.5 million barrels per day above its pre-war level,” they continued. “But here is the rub - the world may have more than enough crude oil to meet demand, but not enough refining capacity to turn it into the products consumers actually need,” they warned. The analysts highlighted that accommodating the additional 1.5 million barrels per day of consumption would require global refinery runs to increase by 1.1 million barrels per day relative to 2025. “Yet global refining capacity is expected to increase by just 0.97 million barrels per day - enough to support an increase in runs of only about 200,000 barrels per day,” they said. “The resulting mismatch between rebounding demand and constrained processing capacity would push gasoline, diesel and jet fuel cracks higher, raising prices for the very products whose soaring costs drove demand down in the first place,” they warned. After accounting for the volume of crude that refiners “can realistically process”, the analysts estimated in the report that global oil demand in 2027 could rise by a maximum of 0.58 million barrels per day above 2025 levels, equivalent to a recovery of 3.5 million barrels per day from 2026. In a BMI report sent to Rigzone by the Fitch Group recently, analysts at BMI, a unit of Fitch Solutions, projected that energy prices are set to fall “as scarcity shifts to oversupply, while refined fuel prices remain elevated”. “After a preliminary U.S.-Iran deal is reached, regional oil and gas flows will rise, paving the way for strong gains in global crude and natural gas exports,” the BMI analysts projected in this report. “As supply growth overwhelms demand, the market will tip into surplus, driving steep and broad-based declines in energy prices,” they added. “That said, global fuel prices will stay elevated into 2027 as refining constraints and record-low inventories keep markets undersupplied, despite improving Strait of Hormuz trade flows and possible extra Mainland Chinese exports,” they continued. The analysts warned in the report that the year 2027 will mark a “sharp reversal” for energy commodities, “as fading geopolitical risk premia and a surge in supply drive steep price declines across the complex”. “The U.S.-Iran war has been the dominant factor behind 2026’s rally, and our core view sees Washington and Tehran reach a preliminary deal in Q1 2027, triggering a sharp sell-off in oil and gas prices,” they said. “As the maritime security environment improves and the Strait of Hormuz reopens, regional flows will normalize in full, unlocking volumes constrained since the outbreak of the conflict,” they added. The BMI analysts noted that Middle Eastern Gulf crude oil producers were operating around seven million barrels per day below capacity as of October 2026 and revealed that they are forecasting that regional production will rise by 5.59 million barrels per day year on year in 2027, “alongside a further 2.10 million barrels per day of growth elsewhere, with the U.S. leading the gains”. “That expansion will comfortably outstrip the recovery in oil demand,” they warned. “Lower energy costs, improving economic conditions, higher Asian refinery utilization and the rebuilding of depleted inventories will absorb some of the additional barrels, but only temporarily, while structural trends towards efficiency, fuel-switching and electrification continue to cap consumption growth,” they projected. The analysts revealed in the report that they expect Brent to average $112 per barrel in Q1 2027 before dropping to $67 per barrel by Q4 2027, averaging $81 per barrel over 2027, “down from $93 per barrel in 2026”. They warned, however, that they are already seeing “strong downside risks to this forecast” which they said they are likely to revise down in the coming weeks. “The emerging glut will test OPEC+’s ability to manage the market and, with the imbalance unlikely to clear in 2028, we forecast Brent to average around $70 per barrel over 2028-2030, with risks tilted towards a deeper downturn,” they said in the report. The BMI analysts projected that refined fuels will fall in tandem but forecasted that “the slower recovery in Middle Eastern downstream operations and continued disruption to Russian refining will keep product cracks historically elevated”. “The same dynamics will play out in gas, as recovering Middle Eastern LNG exports coincide with nearly 95 million tons per annum (mtpa) of new liquefaction capacity by end-2027, pushing global gas markets into prolonged surplus,” they noted. In the report, the BMI analysts went on to highlight that global fuel prices are expected to remain elevated as refining capacity constraints continue to limit supply growth against record-low inventories. “The availability of global refined fuels should continue to steadily improve with increased trade flows emanating from the Strait of Hormuz over the early quarters of 2027, although fundamentals will remain tilted to undersupply, full normalization of pre-conflict trade remains elusive, and Russian refining capacity remains disrupted,” they said. “Mainland China’s increasing fuel exports may give markets some additional supply relief, but limited fuel exports to end-2026 hint at continued restraint for 2027,” they warned. “Diesel, gasoline and jet fuel prices are al forecast to ease from their 2026 peaks but remain elevated through 2027 as refining constraints and depleted inventories keep markets undersupplied,” they added. The analysts outlined in the report that a preliminary U.S.-Iran agreement reopening the Strait of Hormuz in Q1 2027 would support a gradual improvement in product availability but said full normalization of pre-conflict trade flows “will take longer given depleted inventories and constrained refining capacity”. “Additional Mainland Chinese fuel exports could offer some supply relief, but limited export volumes to end-2026 point to continued restraint into 2027,” they projected.
